reverse_outline.summary: Three takeaways: own the joins and cost options over three years, migrate one seam at a time across stages, name an owner for every system and agent
Adding a channel or location changes the business's shape, forcing a choice between leaving systems as they are and replacing them
Kestrel & Pine's systems were bought one at a time from 2016 to 2025, which explains their jobs and gaps
The five 2027 questions the part answers, with the Waypoint program as the case
The questions are about ownership, timing and capacity: decide when the shape changes and move one seam at a time
Build-buy-assemble chapter: compare options by three-year full cost and keep the shop platform
Migration chapter: limited side-by-side transitions, channels on separate dates, freeze around Black Friday
Scaling-stages chapter: business changes that invalidate a design and a stage map of leftover systems
Organizing chapter: an ownership map for systems, integrations and apps, with 13 of 34 integrations found unowned
AI chapter: recommending versus acting AI, data before agents, and agents owned like integrations with no write scope
Ask who owns each shared fact and join after any change, and start with the build-buy chapter

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All ten summaries match their aligned spec paragraphs' controlling ideas in spec order; the KEY POINTS callout is evidence of p04.
The outliner marked no unit two_ideas.
p01-p04 perform the part opening (hook, bridge, questions, claim); p05-p09 each introduce the chapter arguing P10-1 to P10-5; p10 synthesizes.

Each figure's caption says what it shows; the 13 of 34 inventory is explained as 'the joins themselves'; the February pitches are tied to the rebuild question; the 2029 review and Black Friday freeze are explained in their sentences.

Every boundary expresses its declared relationship: time ('Over time'), cause_effect ('That history raises'), elaboration ('None of the five'), section elaboration ('First comes whether to rebuild'), cause_effect ('Added capabilities need'), elaboration ('steps back to the stage that made both due'), sequence ('Next, who keeps', 'The newest writer is AI'), conclusion_summary, and the hand-off 'Begin with [[build-buy-or-assemble]]'.

results.quote: [[commerce-scaling-stages]] steps back to the stage that made both due
results.finding: Both readers found the stages chapter's third position unclear (B: 'Unclear'; A: 'its place is unclear') because Figure 2's loop starts at the stage while the chapters put it third, and neither perceived the declared prerequisite order (A and B read calendar/question order). This is the third round the point recurs; the opening sentence the spec prescribes does not resolve it. The difficulty comes from the declared order set against the author's Figure 2 (and the draft never states the section's idea that each chapter needs what the one before settled); the author must decide between reordering, redrawing Figure 2 or stating the chain.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 2 ('Chapters in this part ... Unclear') and item 3 (Figure 2 vs chapter order); flow reader A item 2 and item 3 (Figure 2 and the text disagree)

results.quote: Over time, those systems arrived between 2016 and 2025, each bought for the business of its year, which explains its jobs and gaps.
results.finding: Both readers re-read this sentence: 'which explains its jobs and gaps' has no clear referent and 'Over time' jars after 'at one moment'.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3 bullet 1 (same sentence); flow reader A, item 3 bullet 3

results.quote: which growth stage to design for and which older systems to retire
results.finding: Both readers miscounted the five questions because the third item holds two clauses; the list needs punctuation or wording that makes five items countable.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3 bullet 2 ('I counted six'); flow reader A, item 3 bullet 4

results.quote: with the old owner kept operable through one peak
results.finding: Both readers stumbled over 'the old owner' (person or system?) and 'one peak'; the body never backs the phrase since 'old paths retire after the peak' was cut. The callout is the author's; the fix belongs in the body (p06) or with the author.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3 bullet 7; flow reader A, item 3 bullet 2

results.quote: Each chapter's case is **Waypoint**, Kestrel & Pine's improvement program.
results.finding: Flow reader A: Waypoint is never mentioned again and reads as a dangling name.

results.quote: First comes whether to rebuild, which two pitches raised in February 2027.
results.finding: Flow reader A: 'the two pitches' are introduced cold (the terms reader also asked who pitched what).
Flow reader B: 'writer' appears in the body only in Figure 2's caption while the body speaks of owners, so the opener feels unearned.

results.quote: Added capabilities need data and orders moved in
results.finding: Flow reader B paused over the compressed 'moved in'.

results.quote: no write scope on stock, prices or orders
results.finding: 'Write scope' is not on already_knows and is never glossed (terms reader item 5); permission jargon for readers new to commerce architecture. Only one reader reported it.

results.quote: Contracts and small-team practices keep each row owned.
results.finding: Terms reader item 10: 'Contracts' is ambiguous (supplier contracts or interface contracts); the spec means supplier contracts. Only one reader reported it.
Opens on a puzzling scenario (a merchant that adds a channel), not a placeholder, restated question, definition, dawn-of-man or book report.
Short closing: one question across the chapters and a course of action; no new idea, no 'in conclusion', no body evidence.
States the one question every chapter asks of its decision (no single paragraph says so) and gives the so-what: the reader can ask it of any proposal.
'A merchant that has just added a store or a channel' returns to p01's merchant.

The AC-1 reader names all five chapters in order with their decisions and Waypoint cases (three-year cost and 2029 review; separate channel dates and Black Friday freeze; stage map; 13 of 34 unowned; data and interfaces before agents). Only 'product publication moves gradually' and 'accountability' from expected are absent, cut by decision. The intro reader predicted the five chapters in the roadmap order, the fictional-case evidence and the tone.

The reader explains growth in jumps, systems bought at different times, problems in the joins, ownership of each fact and join, and timing (decide at the change of shape, one seam at a time, freeze around the peak), matching expected; 'build the differentiating, buy the common' is implied only via the joins.
